# Fine-tuning


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

Fine-tuning trains LoRA adapters with
[mlx-lm](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm) on Haiku’s messages. Each
model is trained on 50, 100 and 199 examples, and scored on the frozen
test set with the code checks, like the [baseline](05_baseline.ipynb);
the scores against the number of examples form the learning curve of the
[scope](design/scope.ipynb).

## Training data

[`teacher_rows`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/finetune.html#teacher_rows)
keeps Haiku’s messages that passed every check, in one fixed random
order. A training set of `n` examples is the first `n` rows, so each
smaller set is part of the larger ones and the curve reflects size, not
a different draw:

    (199, 30)

The fine-tuned models get a one-line instruction, `SHORT_PROMPT`,
instead of the baseline’s student prompt, for two reasons. Training on
Qwen3.5 with the student prompt ran out of memory on a 32 GB M5, even
one example at a time: an example with the full prompt is 1,304 tokens,
and the memory that training needs grows steeply with length. With the
short prompt an example is about 165 tokens and trains easily. On the
board, a short prompt also saves reading 1,300 tokens before every
message. The model learns the rules from the examples instead of reading
them, which is what fine-tuning is for.

mlx-lm reads chat rows: the instruction as the system message, the
record as the user message, and the teacher’s message as the reply.
Qwen3.5’s chat template writes the reply after the same empty thinking
block that
[`student_input`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/baseline.html#student_input)
ends with, so training text starts exactly with the text the model sees
at inference:

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/franckalbinet/edgeslm/blob/main/edgeslm/finetune.py#L39"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

## Training

[`lora_cmd`](https://franckalbinet.github.io/edgeslm/finetune.html#lora_cmd)
builds the command that runs mlx-lm’s trainer as a separate process.
Every run uses the same settings: mlx-lm’s default rank, layers and
maximum length, a learning rate of 1e-4, and 4 epochs. Training Qwen3.5
in mlx-lm takes far more memory than a model of this size should:
batches of 4 short examples, about 1,200 tokens, ran out of memory on a
32 GB M5. Each step therefore takes one example, with gradient
checkpointing, and the weights update every 4 steps, which matches
batches of 4 for the optimiser. Only the reply counts in the loss, and
validation runs once per epoch:

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/franckalbinet/edgeslm/blob/main/edgeslm/finetune.py#L50"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### lora_cmd

``` python
def lora_cmd(
    model_id:str, # Hugging Face id of the MLX model
    data:str, # Directory written by `write_mlx_data`
    adapters:str, # Directory for the trained adapters
    n:int, # Number of training examples
    accum:int=4, # Examples per weight update, one at a time
    epochs:int=4, # Passes over the training set
    lr:float=0.0001, # Learning rate
)->list: # The command, as arguments for `subprocess.run`
```

*The mlx-lm command that trains LoRA adapters for `model_id` on `data`*

This cell trained the six adapters and scored each one on the test set,
and does not run in tests. On an Apple M5 with 32 GB, training took
about 2 hours and scoring about 80 minutes. The 2B on 199 examples took
65 minutes to train and 37 to score, against 13 and 12 for the 2B on 100
examples. We have not found the cause of that slowdown yet:

``` python
import re
test = read_jsonl('../data/test-v1.jsonl')
MODELS = {'qwen3.5-0.8b': 'mlx-community/Qwen3.5-0.8B-bf16', 'qwen3.5-2b': 'mlx-community/Qwen3.5-2B-bf16'}
for name, mid in MODELS.items():
    for n in (50, 100, 199):
        run = f'{name}-n{n}'
        write_mlx_data(f'../models/{run}/data', train[:n], valid)
        res = subprocess.run(lora_cmd(mid, f'../models/{run}/data', f'../models/{run}/adapters', n), capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
        Path(f'../models/{run}/train.log').write_text(re.sub(r'\x1b\[[0-9;?]*[A-Za-z]', '', res.stdout))
        write_jsonl(f'../data/finetune-v1-{run}.jsonl', run_model(mid, test, adapter_path=f'../models/{run}/adapters', sp=SHORT_PROMPT))
```

With 100 examples, both models pass every check in 255 or more of the
270 messages, against 123 for the untuned 0.8B and 70 for the untuned
2B. With 199 examples the 0.8B reaches 264, and the 2B falls back to
250.

With 50 examples, the 0.8B scores below its baseline. It mixes up
locations and repeats them (“plant 2, plant 2 … plants 2, 2 and 3”), 41
of its messages repeat one phrase until the token limit, and some
contain a stray `</think>` tag. The 2B on 50 examples has none of these
failures and passes 229.

We scored the adapter saved at the end of the fourth epoch. Validation
loss after each epoch, from `models/<run>/train.log`:

The 2B on 199 examples has the largest rise in the last epoch, from
0.062 to 0.104. Its drop in score is consistent with overfitting in that
epoch. Scoring its third-epoch adapter would test this.

Fine-tuning teaches the severity-to-marker mapping that the prompt did
not. The 0.8B on 199 examples writes the right marker for all 469 test
items. In the pairs below, `None` marks an item whose location the model
wrote differently from the record:

``` python
markers(runs['0.8b n199'], test), markers(runs['2b n100'], test)
```
